purpose: This medicine is used to treat certain types of breast cancer and stomach cancer that have too much of a protein called HER2. It is a biosimilar, meaning it works just like the original trastuzumab (Herceptin) but is made by a different manufacturer. Your doctor may use it alone or together with other cancer medicines.
how_it_works: Your cancer cells have a protein on their surface called HER2 that tells them to grow out of control. This medicine acts like a smart missile — it attaches directly to that HER2 protein and blocks it from sending those grow signals. It also helps your own immune system recognize and attack the cancer cells.
common_side_effects: Feeling tired, nausea, headache, diarrhea, chills, fever, and muscle or joint pain are common. Some people notice hair thinning or skin rash. You might also have reactions during or right after the infusion, like flushing, dizziness, or shortness of breath.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious heart problems, including weakening of the heart muscle, so your doctor will monitor your heart regularly. It should NOT be used during pregnancy because it can seriously harm an unborn baby — use reliable birth control. Lung problems, including severe breathing difficulty, can also occur. Tell your doctor right away if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, swelling in your legs, or sudden weight gain.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given by IV infusion (directly into a vein) at a clinic or hospital, usually once every 1 or 3 weeks depending on your treatment plan. The first infusion is given slowly over about 90 minutes; if you tolerate it well, later infusions may be given over 30 minutes. Your doctor will decide the exact dose based on your weight and the type of cancer being treated.
